families.topic: reservoir, geographic risk, transmission, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment and prevention of MERS-CoV
evidence_points: MERS-CoV is a zoonotic respiratory virus associated primarily with dromedary camels.
Human cases have been reported mainly from the Middle East.
Camel contact and raw camel products are recognised risk factors.
Limited person-to-person transmission can occur in households and healthcare settings.
Clinical presentations range from asymptomatic infection to severe pneumonia and multi-organ failure.
Risk of severe disease is higher in older adults and people with chronic conditions.
Laboratory diagnosis uses reverse-transcriptase PCR for viral RNA.
There is no licensed vaccine or specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive.
Travel to the Middle East alone does not establish a suspected MERS case.
Assessment requires symptoms, travel dates, camel or healthcare exposure, contact history and laboratory testing.

families.topic: current UK and traveller risk assessment, monitoring and prevention recommendations for MERS-CoV
evidence_points: UKHSA monitors MERS-CoV developments in the Middle East and internationally.
The assessment is updated when epidemiology or recommendations change.
The May 2026 assessment describes the traveller risk for the Middle East as very low.
The May 2026 assessment describes the risk of acquiring MERS-CoV in the UK as extremely low.
Risk advice includes avoiding relevant camel exposures and following travel-health recommendations.
Healthcare-associated transmission remains an important scenario in affected regions.
Imported cases remain possible because international travel continues.
UKHSA liaises with international partners when reviewing the risk.
A population-level risk rating does not determine the risk for an individual symptomatic traveller.
Individual assessment requires destination, dates, exposures, symptoms, contacts and current epidemiology.

families.source: HCAI operational guidance and standards for health protection teams
families.topic: health-protection actions, governance and partnership responsibilities for healthcare-associated infection risk
families.page_title: Healthcare associated infection (HCAI): operational guidance and standards
evidence_points: The guidance describes actions health protection teams should take to reduce healthcare-associated infection risk.
It applies to local health and social care settings.
It defines operational expectations for health protection staff.
It describes governance arrangements supporting HCAI responsibilities.
It emphasises partnership with providers, commissioners, regulators and performance managers.
It supports coordinated incident advice and risk reduction.
It provides a framework for local and regional HCAI work.
It should be used with current organism-specific and infection-control guidance.
The existence of an infection in a healthcare setting does not automatically prove healthcare acquisition.
Assessment requires timing, procedures, exposure pathways, microbiology, epidemiology and organisational evidence.

families.source: UKHSA surgical site infection surveillance protocol and guides
families.topic: standardised SSI definitions, procedure coding, data collection and hospital surveillance methods
families.page_title: Surgical site infection surveillance service: protocol and guides
evidence_points: The publication provides the national protocol for surgical site infection surveillance.
It includes operating procedure codes used to select eligible surgical categories.
It supports consistent recording of surgical site infection incidents.
It is designed for hospital staff participating in the surveillance service.
The protocol standardises the minimum data needed for surveillance.
It supports data quality and comparison across participating hospitals.
It enables hospitals to analyse infection rates and review practice.
It is used with the web-based UKHSA surveillance system and local governance.
A postoperative wound concern does not automatically meet a surveillance case definition.
Classification requires procedure eligibility, timing, clinical signs, microbiology and protocol-defined criteria.

families.source: UKHSA infection prevention and control guidance for multidrug-resistant organisms in adult social care
families.topic: MDRO carriage, communication, admission, hand hygiene, cleaning, equipment and dignity-preserving IPC
families.page_title: Infection prevention and control for multidrug-resistant organisms in adult social care settings
evidence_points: The guidance applies to staff and managers across adult social care settings.
Multidrug-resistant organisms can spread through direct contact and contaminated surfaces or equipment.
People with wounds, devices or weakened immunity can have greater infection risk.
Carriage without symptoms is common and may persist for years.
Admission or readmission should not usually be denied solely because of MDRO carriage.
Hand hygiene, PPE, environmental cleaning and equipment decontamination reduce transmission risk.
Known carriage should be communicated safely during transfers between care and healthcare services.
IPC measures should balance safety with dignity, autonomy and social inclusion.
MDRO carriage is not the same as symptomatic infection and does not require automatic isolation from normal life.
Precautions require individual risk assessment, care activities, wounds or devices, environment and specialist IPC advice.
